prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You whom I could not save Listen to me. Try to understand this simple speech as I would be ashamed of another. I swear, there is in me no wizardry of words. I speak to you with silence like a cloud or a tree. What strengthened me, for you was lethal. You mixed up farewell to an epoch with the beginning of a new one, Inspiration of hatred with lyrical beauty; Blind force with accomplished shape. Here is a valley of shallow Polish rivers. And an immense bridge Going into white fog. Here is a broken city; And the wind throws the screams of gulls on your grave When I am talking with you. What is poetry which does not save Nations or people? A connivance with official lies, A song of drunkards whose throats will be cut in a moment, Readings for sophomore girls. That I wanted good poetry without knowing it, That I discovered, late, its salutary aim, In this and only this I find salvation. They used to pour millet on graves or poppy seeds To feed the dead who would come disguised as birds. I put this book here for you, who once lived So that you should visit us no more. Warsaw, 1945

outputs.L1:
You whom I could not save,  
listen to me.  
Try to understand this simple speech,  
for I would be ashamed of any other.  
I swear there is no wizardry of words in me.  
I speak to you through silence,  
like a cloud or a tree.

What strengthened me proved lethal to you.  
You confused the farewell to an epoch  
with the beginning of a new one;  
the inspiration of hatred with lyrical beauty;  
blind force with accomplished form.

Here is a valley of shallow Polish rivers,  
and an immense bridge  
vanishing into white fog.  
Here is a broken city,  
and the wind casts the cries of gulls upon your grave  
as I speak with you.

What is poetry that saves  
neither nations nor people?  
A connivance with official lies,  
a song of drunkards whose throats will soon be cut,  
reading for sophomore girls.

That I sought good poetry without knowing it,  
that I discovered—late—its power to save:  
in this, and this alone, I find salvation.

They once scattered millet or poppy seeds upon graves  
to feed the dead, who would return disguised as birds.  
I place this book here for you, who once lived,  
so that you may visit us no more.

**Warsaw, 1945**
outputs.L2:
You, whom I was powerless to rescue,  
hear me now. Make an effort to grasp these plain words,  
because any more elaborate language would shame me.  
I promise I possess no verbal enchantment.  
I address you wordlessly,  
as a tree or a cloud might.

The very thing that gave me strength  
brought about your destruction.  
You mistook an age’s ending  
for the arrival of another;  
you confused hatred’s fervor with poetic grace,  
and brute power with perfected form.

Before us lies a lowland crossed by Poland’s shallow rivers,  
and a vast bridge disappearing into pale mist.  
Here stands a city reduced to ruins.  
As I speak with you, the wind scatters the cries of seagulls  
over your grave.

What value can poetry have  
if it rescues neither individuals nor nations?  
Then it merely tolerates state-sanctioned falsehoods,  
becomes the singing of drunken men soon to be slaughtered,  
or material assigned to schoolgirls.

My redemption lies in this alone:  
without realizing it, I sought poetry that was good,  
and only much later understood  
that its purpose is to bring deliverance.

In former times, people scattered millet or poppy seeds on graves,  
offering food to the dead  
when they returned in the bodies of birds.  
For you, who once belonged among the living,  
I leave this book here,  
so that you will not come back to haunt us.

Warsaw, 1945
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses those he was unable to save, using plain, restrained language rather than elaborate poetic ornament. This simplicity reflects both the depth of his grief and his sense that beautiful language would be inadequate—or even inappropriate—in the face of such suffering. He recalls how others mistook hatred and destructive force for beauty, renewal, and artistic form, transforming violence into something falsely noble or aesthetically appealing.

Images of a shattered Warsaw, a bridge hidden by fog, and graves scattered across the devastated landscape evoke the immense destruction and sorrow left by war. Against this background, the speaker questions the value of poetry itself. He condemns poetry that cannot save people or nations, regarding art that ignores reality as morally compromised and potentially complicit in deception and approaching violence.

Yet the poem does not completely reject poetry. Instead, the speaker comes to recognize its moral and healing purpose: poetry must bear witness, preserve memory, and resist the lies that make destruction possible. By offering his book to the dead, he turns it into both a tribute and a farewell. The gesture acknowledges his failure to save them while affirming his responsibility to remember them and speak honestly about what they endured.
outputs.L4:
Addressing those whom he was unable to save, the poet speaks with humility and guilt, rejecting ornate language in favor of a direct, unadorned voice. Against the bleak postwar landscape of shallow Polish rivers, a bridge disappearing into fog, and the ruins of Warsaw, he reflects on the failure of art and on his own survival. The dead had mistaken the end of an era for the beginning of a better one, confusing hatred with inspiration and blind violence with artistic form. The poet, meanwhile, remains alive to speak beside their graves, yet his words cannot undo their suffering.

This sense of inadequacy leads him to ask what value poetry can have if it does not help save nations or individual human beings. Poetry that merely accommodates official falsehoods, beautifies violence, or distracts people awaiting destruction is morally empty. He therefore recognizes that poetry has an ethical obligation: it must oppose lies, preserve truth, and defend human life and memory. Although he arrived at this understanding too late to rescue the dead, he finds a measure of personal redemption in finally grasping poetry’s “salutary aim.”

The book itself becomes an offering. Recalling the ancient custom of leaving grain on graves to nourish the dead when they returned in the form of birds, the poet places his poems before those who once lived. In doing so, he creates both a memorial and an act of farewell. The poems cannot restore the victims, but they can bear witness to them, resist their erasure, and perhaps allow the living—and the poet himself—to move beyond guilt toward a belated form of salvation.
